title: Tansuo t01: Follow a Tap into a Chip · 音频预览
tagline: 出视频前的整集听感：本地 VoxCPM2 按人物声样模拟对白，无画面、无配乐、无音效；每镜时长与台词起点就是之后出视频的目标。

items.title: s1 · 城市错觉拉远
items.subtitle: 阿凯：...A city? Like looking down from a plane at night? / 阿凯：...No way. This is a chip?
items.detail: 本镜 9 秒（口播加起收需要 8.7 秒）；台词起点 1.5s、5.4s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s2-1 · 芯片特写
items.subtitle: 阿凯：A chip this small can hold nineteen billion switches? That's more than two for every person on Earth. But even with my eye practically touching it, I can't see a single one.
items.detail: 本镜 11 秒（口播加起收需要 10.5 秒）；台词起点 0.4s
items.note: 临时沿用 P01 作构图参考，不代表本镜已审通过；后期小字：数量举例：2023 年 A17 Pro，190 亿晶体管；不是画中无品牌样品的实测。

items.title: s2-2 · 晶体管定义
items.subtitle: 林工：It's true. These tiny switches are called transistors. A chip is a tiny slice packed with enormous numbers of them. / 阿凯：Okay... I'll believe half of that for now.
items.detail: 本镜 11 秒（口播加起收需要 10.7 秒）；台词起点 0.4s、7.8s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s3-1 · 点击手机
items.subtitle: 阿凯：See? One tap, and it lights up. But what's actually happening in there when I tap? / 林工：Let's follow that tap inside and find one of the switches it flips.
items.detail: 本镜 10 秒（口播加起收需要 9.2 秒）；台词起点 0.4s、4.9s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s3-2 · 缩小规则
items.subtitle: 林工：Each click makes us ten times smaller. We'll shrink to see the switches, then magnify the view to see atoms. / 阿凯：Hang on. How small are we talking? I'm not ready for this—
items.detail: 本镜 12 秒（口播加起收需要 11.3 秒）；台词起点 0.4s、6.9s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图；后期标注：缩小旅行／信号放慢为叙事示意；一次点击涉及许多器件，并非只拨动一个开关。

items.title: s4 · 米粒与头发
items.subtitle: 阿凯：Whoa, that grain of rice is like a mountain. And that cliff next to it... don't tell me that's a hair. / 林工：It's a hair, about 80 to 100 micrometers thick. Follow that blue-white light. That's your tap.
items.detail: 本镜 15 秒（口播加起收需要 14.6 秒）；台词起点 0.6s、6.9s
items.note: 临时沿用 P02 作构图参考，不代表本镜已审通过

items.title: s5 · 黑色封装
items.subtitle: 阿凯：That black block is the chip, right? It looks more like a chip than anything else on the board. / 林工：Close. That's the package, basically its protective case. The actual chip is the thin slice of silicon inside.
items.detail: 本镜 15 秒（口播加起收需要 14.7 秒）；台词起点 0.4s、6.4s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s6-1 · 焊球大厅
items.subtitle: 阿凯：Whoa, it's like an underground parking garage. What are all these shiny balls for, and why are there so many?
items.detail: 本镜 8 秒（口播加起收需要 7.2 秒）；台词起点 0.4s
items.note: 临时沿用 P03 作构图参考，不代表本镜已审通过

items.title: s6-2 · 焊球连接
items.subtitle: 林工：Those are solder balls, the doorways between the chip and the motherboard. Power comes in through them, and signals go in and out.
items.detail: 本镜 9 秒（口播加起收需要 8.8 秒）；台词起点 0.4s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s6-3 · 供电接地与数据
items.subtitle: 林工：We need so many to supply power, complete circuits, and carry data—not just to connect different parts.
items.detail: 本镜 8 秒（口播加起收需要 7.2 秒）；台词起点 0.4s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s7-1 · 封装爆炸分解
items.subtitle: 阿凯：Oh, it's opening up. So this thin gray slice is the actual chip? Why is it lying face-down? / 林工：It's mounted upside down. The side with switches and wiring faces the motherboard, and that's where power and signals go in and out.
items.detail: 本镜 15 秒（口播加起收需要 14.7 秒）；台词起点 0.6s、6.5s
items.note: 临时沿用 P04 作构图参考，不代表本镜已审通过

items.title: s7-2 · 硅片翻转
items.subtitle: 阿凯：Then we need to flip it over. / 林工：Okay, let's flip it so we can see. Just to be clear, a real chip doesn't do that.
items.detail: 本镜 8 秒（口播加起收需要 7.8 秒）；台词起点 0.4s、2.2s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s8-1 · 硅片城市
items.subtitle: 阿凯：It really does look like a city from a plane. Which part is the CPU? / 林工：This is the CPU. Let's skip the other names and focus on what these regions share: the switches at the bottom.
items.detail: 本镜 12 秒（口播加起收需要 11.9 秒）；台词起点 0.4s、4.5s
items.note: 临时沿用 P05 作构图参考，不代表本镜已审通过

items.title: s8-2 · 颜色是后加的
items.subtitle: 林工：But honestly, you couldn't tell these regions apart from up here. We added these colors ourselves. / 阿凯：Wait, you added them?
items.detail: 本镜 8 秒（口播加起收需要 7.9 秒）；台词起点 0.4s、5.7s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s9-1 · 开关在哪个区
items.subtitle: 阿凯：So which area has the switches? / 林工：All these areas run on transistors. Different components and connections do different jobs. / 阿凯：Then why haven't I seen a single one since we got here?
items.detail: 本镜 12 秒（口播加起收需要 11.4 秒）；台词起点 0.4s、2.6s、7.8s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s9-2 · 开关在最底下
items.subtitle: 林工：Because they're at the very bottom, under more than a dozen layers of wiring. Let's head down.
items.detail: 本镜 7 秒（口播加起收需要 6.2 秒）；台词起点 0.4s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s10-1 · 导线城市
items.subtitle: 阿凯：All these layers look like highway overpasses. These must be the switches, right? / 林工：Nope, these are wires, mostly copper. There are more than a dozen layers.
items.detail: 本镜 13 秒（口播加起收需要 12.5 秒）；台词起点 1.2s、6.5s
items.note: 临时沿用 P06 作构图参考，不代表本镜已审通过；首次进结构层上屏：多种先进工艺的结构示例，非同一型号复刻 / Examples from different processes; not one chip teardown。

items.title: s10-2 · 上粗下细
items.subtitle: 林工：Up top, long, thick routes carry power and signals like highways. Below, short, narrow connections near the switches form crowded alleys.
items.detail: 本镜 11 秒（口播加起收需要 10.3 秒）；台词起点 0.4s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s10-3 · 层间绝缘与通孔
items.subtitle: 林工：Insulating material separates the layers, so crossing wires don't short out. Neighboring layers often run in different directions to make routing easier. Short posts connect the layers where needed.
items.detail: 本镜 13 秒（口播加起收需要 12.1 秒）；台词起点 0.4s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s11-1 · 信号与电子
items.subtitle: 阿凯：Look at that light go. It just zipped around the corner. The electrons must be racing through there, right? / 林工：See those little orange dots in the wire? Those are the electrons. They don't travel along with that light.
items.detail: 本镜 13 秒（口播加起收需要 12.7 秒）；台词起点 0.4s、6.0s
items.note: 临时沿用 P07 作构图参考，不代表本镜已审通过

items.title: s11-2 · 电子只挪一点
items.subtitle: 林工：The electrons jiggle in place and drift slightly. The electric field carries that push forward much faster. / 阿凯：Oh, like a packed subway: everyone shifts a little. But electric fields, not collisions, carry the change, which takes time.
items.detail: 本镜 15 秒（口播加起收需要 14.9 秒）；台词起点 0.4s、6.4s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s12-1 · 拍糊了
items.subtitle: 阿凯：I have to get a picture of this... Huh? Why is it all blurry? Come on, focus! / 林工：Your phone isn't the problem. Light itself is too blunt a tool for this.
items.detail: 本镜 10 秒（口播加起收需要 9.9 秒）；台词起点 0.4s、5.0s
items.note: 临时沿用 P08 作构图参考，不代表本镜已审通过

items.title: s12-2 · 光的波长太粗
items.subtitle: 林工：Visible light spans 400 to 700 nanometers. Here, neighboring wire and transistor features have center-to-center spacing of tens of nanometers, so ordinary optical microscopes struggle to resolve them. More magnification won't help.
items.detail: 本镜 15 秒（口播加起收需要 14.5 秒）；台词起点 0.4s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s12-3 · 电子显微镜灰图示意
items.subtitle: 林工：Engineers use electron microscopes here, and the raw pictures are gray. We added colors to the chip's materials so we can tell them apart.
items.detail: 本镜 10 秒（口播加起收需要 9.0 秒）；台词起点 0.4s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s12-4 · 全灰了
items.subtitle: 阿凯：...Whoa, it's all gray. So that's an electron-microscope image. Like an old photograph.
items.detail: 本镜 8 秒（口播加起收需要 7.4 秒）；台词起点 0.4s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s13-1 · 抵达栅极阵列
items.subtitle: 阿凯：Finally, the bottom. Hey, people always talk about three nanometers. Which part is three nanometers, these walls or the gaps between them?
items.detail: 本镜 9 秒（口播加起收需要 8.2 秒）；台词起点 0.4s
items.note: 临时沿用 P09 作构图参考，不代表本镜已审通过

items.title: s13-2 · 栅极中心间距
items.subtitle: 林工：In one advanced process, these walls are called gates. Their centers are about 50 nanometers apart, so 1,600 to 2,000 gates could fit side by side across one hair.
items.detail: 本镜 13 秒（口播加起收需要 12.1 秒）；台词起点 0.4s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图；标尺：栅极中心距约 50 nm，仅为一种工艺示例；线宽、缝宽不能代替中心距。

items.title: s13-3 · 工艺代号
items.subtitle: 林工：So don't expect to measure three nanometers with a ruler here. It's a process name, like a car model. It doesn't match any single edge.
items.detail: 本镜 10 秒（口播加起收需要 9.5 秒）；台词起点 0.4s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图；短字卡：工艺代号 ≠ 单一尺寸 / Process name ≠ one dimension。

items.title: s14-1 · 发现一个开关
items.subtitle: 阿凯：This is a switch? Shouldn't a switch have some kind of handle? But nothing's moving. How does it turn on and off?
items.detail: 本镜 8 秒（口播加起收需要 7.4 秒）；台词起点 0.4s
items.note: 临时沿用 P10 作构图参考，不代表本镜已审通过

items.title: s14-2 · 纳米片结构
items.subtitle: 林工：Picture an advanced nanosheet switch. Three or four super-thin silicon sheets, each about six nanometers thick, connect the two ends. The gate wraps around every sheet.
items.detail: 本镜 12 秒（口播加起收需要 11.8 秒）；台词起点 0.4s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图；模型切换卡：纳米片晶体管示意 / Nanosheet transistor example；不宣称开场 A17 Pro 使用环绕栅。

items.title: s14-3 · 继电器对比
items.subtitle: 林工：That handle you want? Some early computers did have something like that. They used relays. Apply power, and an electromagnet pulls a piece of iron over. Click—the contacts touch.
items.detail: 本镜 15 秒（口播加起收需要 14.5 秒）；台词起点 0.4s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s14-4 · 没有机械零件
items.subtitle: 林工：But here, not a single part moves. / 阿凯：No mechanical parts move at all... Does it still count as a switch?
items.detail: 本镜 8 秒（口播加起收需要 7.9 秒）；台词起点 0.4s、3.3s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s15-1 · 关态
items.subtitle: 林工：This N-type transistor is normally off. Why? / 阿凯：But with no gate voltage, doesn't silicon still have electrons?
items.detail: 本镜 10 秒（口播加起收需要 9.2 秒）；台词起点 1.0s、4.8s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图；屏幕仅显示短角标：增强型 N 沟道示例 / Enhancement-mode nMOS。制作要求（不上屏）：这里的栅压均相对源极；源漏已有电势差，栅压控制通道；电子来自源漏载流子库，不画成绝缘层漏进来的电子。

items.title: s15-2 · 断的是通道不是材料
items.subtitle: 林工：It does, but they haven't formed a channel connecting the two ends. So right now, it's off. / 阿凯：So the silicon stays. It's the path that's missing, not the material?
items.detail: 本镜 11 秒（口播加起收需要 10.2 秒）；台词起点 0.4s、5.8s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s15-3 · 不是铺实体路
items.subtitle: 林工：Right. We're not building a physical road. The silicon stays in place. More electrons make it conductive. Watch the gate do it.
items.detail: 本镜 9 秒（口播加起收需要 8.8 秒）；台词起点 0.4s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s16-1 · 极薄绝缘层
items.subtitle: 林工：A very thin insulator separates the gate from the silicon. The field acts through it, but any gate leakage into the silicon is normally tiny.
items.detail: 本镜 9 秒（口播加起收需要 8.9 秒）；台词起点 0.8s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图；用不同材质明确区分灰色硅、薄绝缘层、栅金属；切面描白边，不画成栅极开窗。

items.title: s16-2 · 加电形成通道
items.subtitle: 林工：Now let's put a voltage on the gate. See? The electric field reaches through the insulator and pulls electrons in the silicon toward the insulating layer.
items.detail: 本镜 10 秒（口播加起收需要 9.5 秒）；台词起点 0.4s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s16-3 · 成通道再撤电
items.subtitle: 林工：More and more electrons gather there and form a continuous channel. The two ends are connected. / 林工：Now take the voltage away. The electrons spread out, the channel disappears, and it's off again.
items.detail: 本镜 14 秒（口播加起收需要 13.8 秒）；台词起点 0.4s、5.9s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s16-4 · 结构不动与隔层追问
items.subtitle: 林工：The whole time, not one mechanical part moved. What changed was the electric field and where the electrons were. / 阿凯：Wait, there's an insulator in the way. The gate can't even touch those electrons, so how can it pull them over?
items.detail: 本镜 14 秒（口播加起收需要 13.8 秒）；台词起点 0.4s、7.8s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s16-5 · 磁铁隔空类比
items.subtitle: 林工：You know how a magnet can move iron filings even through a tabletop? It's pulling without touching them. Something similar is happening here, except this is an electric field, not a magnetic one.
items.detail: 本镜 12 秒（口播加起收需要 11.4 秒）；台词起点 0.4s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s16-6 · 看懂了
items.subtitle: 阿凯：...That's it? I thought there'd be some tiny hidden mechanism in there. / 林工：That's it. Enough positive voltage turns it on. Take it away, and it turns off.
items.detail: 本镜 11 秒（口播加起收需要 10.1 秒）；台词起点 0.4s、4.2s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s17-1 · 为什么四面包住
items.subtitle: 阿凯：It's wrapped up tightly on all four sides. Why go that far? Wouldn't covering one side be enough?
items.detail: 本镜 7 秒（口播加起收需要 6.6 秒）；台词起点 0.4s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s17-2 · 包围与漏电
items.subtitle: 林工：The more the gate wraps, the better it usually controls the channel. Less current leaks when it's off, but off doesn't mean zero current. A tiny amount can get through.
items.detail: 本镜 11 秒（口播加起收需要 10.2 秒）；台词起点 0.4s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s17-3 · 平面到全包
items.subtitle: 林工：That's why the design evolved from flat layers to upright fin channels, and now to gates wrapping all four sides.
items.detail: 本镜 8 秒（口播加起收需要 7.4 秒）；台词起点 0.4s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s18-1 · 点击到了
items.subtitle: 阿凯：Here it comes, that's my tap! ...But what does one switch turning on and off have to do with the photos and messages on my phone?
items.detail: 本镜 8 秒（口播加起收需要 7.8 秒）；台词起点 0.4s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s18-2 · 高低电压与零一
items.subtitle: 林工：In a chip, high and low voltages often represent ones and zeros. Switches turn on and off to create and pass along these signals.
items.detail: 本镜 9 秒（口播加起收需要 8.6 秒）；台词起点 0.4s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图

items.title: s18-3 · 反相器
items.subtitle: 林工：Two different types of switches can work together as an inverter. A one becomes a zero, and a zero becomes a one. An inverter can't store photos by itself. Different circuits work together to make decisions, store photos, and play videos.
items.detail: 本镜 15 秒（口播加起收需要 15.0 秒）；台词起点 0.4s
items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图；画出电源、地、互补 P/N 两管、共用输入与输出；高输入时 N 通 P 断、输出低，低输入相反。

items.title: s18-4 · 信号传向下一开关
items.subtitle: 林工：Your tap reaches the gate: the channel conducts, changing the output voltage. A wire carries that change to the next stage. / 阿凯：So my tap really did make it all the way here... Found you.
items.detail: 本镜 13 秒（口播加起收需要 12.2 秒）；台词起点 0.4s、7.6s
items.note: V18C 历史构图通过独立审图；本轮制作说明仍待复审，不等于结构模型或成片验收

items.title: s19-1 · 数原子

items.note: 首帧待出：本镜有独立机位，不再套用无关旧图；片尾补 AI 生成画面／AI 配音标注及来源卡；下一期：开关怎么组成加法。

cues.text: ...A city? Like looking down from a plane at night?
...No way. This is a chip?
A chip this small can hold nineteen billion switches? That's more than two for every person on Earth. But even with my eye practically touching it, I can't see a single one.
It's true. These tiny switches are called transistors. A chip is a tiny slice packed with enormous numbers of them.
Okay... I'll believe half of that for now.
See? One tap, and it lights up. But what's actually happening in there when I tap?
Let's follow that tap inside and find one of the switches it flips.
Each click makes us ten times smaller. We'll shrink to see the switches, then magnify the view to see atoms.
Hang on. How small are we talking? I'm not ready for this—
Whoa, that grain of rice is like a mountain. And that cliff next to it... don't tell me that's a hair.
It's a hair, about 80 to 100 micrometers thick. Follow that blue-white light. That's your tap.
That black block is the chip, right? It looks more like a chip than anything else on the board.
Close. That's the package, basically its protective case. The actual chip is the thin slice of silicon inside.
Whoa, it's like an underground parking garage. What are all these shiny balls for, and why are there so many?
Those are solder balls, the doorways between the chip and the motherboard. Power comes in through them, and signals go in and out.
We need so many to supply power, complete circuits, and carry data—not just to connect different parts.
Oh, it's opening up. So this thin gray slice is the actual chip? Why is it lying face-down?
It's mounted upside down. The side with switches and wiring faces the motherboard, and that's where power and signals go in and out.
Then we need to flip it over.
Okay, let's flip it so we can see. Just to be clear, a real chip doesn't do that.
It really does look like a city from a plane. Which part is the CPU?
This is the CPU. Let's skip the other names and focus on what these regions share: the switches at the bottom.
But honestly, you couldn't tell these regions apart from up here. We added these colors ourselves.
Wait, you added them?
So which area has the switches?
All these areas run on transistors. Different components and connections do different jobs.
Then why haven't I seen a single one since we got here?
Because they're at the very bottom, under more than a dozen layers of wiring. Let's head down.
All these layers look like highway overpasses. These must be the switches, right?
Nope, these are wires, mostly copper. There are more than a dozen layers.
Up top, long, thick routes carry power and signals like highways. Below, short, narrow connections near the switches form crowded alleys.
Insulating material separates the layers, so crossing wires don't short out. Neighboring layers often run in different directions to make routing easier. Short posts connect the layers where needed.
Look at that light go. It just zipped around the corner. The electrons must be racing through there, right?
See those little orange dots in the wire? Those are the electrons. They don't travel along with that light.
The electrons jiggle in place and drift slightly. The electric field carries that push forward much faster.
Oh, like a packed subway: everyone shifts a little. But electric fields, not collisions, carry the change, which takes time.
I have to get a picture of this... Huh? Why is it all blurry? Come on, focus!
Your phone isn't the problem. Light itself is too blunt a tool for this.

Visible light spans 400 to 700 nanometers. Here, neighboring wire and transistor features have center-to-center spacing of tens of nanometers, so ordinary optical microscopes struggle to resolve them. More magnification won't help.
Engineers use electron microscopes here, and the raw pictures are gray. We added colors to the chip's materials so we can tell them apart.
...Whoa, it's all gray. So that's an electron-microscope image. Like an old photograph.
Finally, the bottom. Hey, people always talk about three nanometers. Which part is three nanometers, these walls or the gaps between them?
In one advanced process, these walls are called gates. Their centers are about 50 nanometers apart, so 1,600 to 2,000 gates could fit side by side across one hair.
So don't expect to measure three nanometers with a ruler here. It's a process name, like a car model. It doesn't match any single edge.
This is a switch? Shouldn't a switch have some kind of handle? But nothing's moving. How does it turn on and off?
Picture an advanced nanosheet switch. Three or four super-thin silicon sheets, each about six nanometers thick, connect the two ends. The gate wraps around every sheet.
That handle you want? Some early computers did have something like that. They used relays. Apply power, and an electromagnet pulls a piece of iron over. Click—the contacts touch.
But here, not a single part moves.
No mechanical parts move at all... Does it still count as a switch?
This N-type transistor is normally off. Why?
But with no gate voltage, doesn't silicon still have electrons?
It does, but they haven't formed a channel connecting the two ends. So right now, it's off.
So the silicon stays. It's the path that's missing, not the material?
Right. We're not building a physical road. The silicon stays in place. More electrons make it conductive. Watch the gate do it.
A very thin insulator separates the gate from the silicon. The field acts through it, but any gate leakage into the silicon is normally tiny.
Now let's put a voltage on the gate. See? The electric field reaches through the insulator and pulls electrons in the silicon toward the insulating layer.
More and more electrons gather there and form a continuous channel. The two ends are connected.
Now take the voltage away. The electrons spread out, the channel disappears, and it's off again.
The whole time, not one mechanical part moved. What changed was the electric field and where the electrons were.
Wait, there's an insulator in the way. The gate can't even touch those electrons, so how can it pull them over?
You know how a magnet can move iron filings even through a tabletop? It's pulling without touching them. Something similar is happening here, except this is an electric field, not a magnetic one.
...That's it? I thought there'd be some tiny hidden mechanism in there.
That's it. Enough positive voltage turns it on. Take it away, and it turns off.
It's wrapped up tightly on all four sides. Why go that far? Wouldn't covering one side be enough?
The more the gate wraps, the better it usually controls the channel. Less current leaks when it's off, but off doesn't mean zero current. A tiny amount can get through.
That's why the design evolved from flat layers to upright fin channels, and now to gates wrapping all four sides.
Here it comes, that's my tap! ...But what does one switch turning on and off have to do with the photos and messages on my phone?
In a chip, high and low voltages often represent ones and zeros. Switches turn on and off to create and pass along these signals.

Two different types of switches can work together as an inverter. A one becomes a zero, and a zero becomes a one. An inverter can't store photos by itself. Different circuits work together to make decisions, store photos, and play videos.
Your tap reaches the gate: the channel conducts, changing the output voltage. A wire carries that change to the next stage.
So my tap really did make it all the way here... Found you.
One, two, three, four... five...
In this six-nanometer example, each sheet is only forty-something atomic layers thick. Engineers really can make silicon sheets this thin.
...Ten or twenty billion switches, made and wired together on a silicon slice.
Guess how much smaller we are now.
Hmm... Ten thousand times? The dial only clicked a few times.
Seven clicks and a bit, each making us ten times smaller. We're about 100 nanometers tall now, seventeen million times smaller than before.
Seventeen million?...
What if we enlarged the chip seventeen million times too? Would each switch take up as much space as we do?
Yes. Each switch would take up just over a square meter on average. The chip would cover about twice Beijing's area. That's how a fingernail-sized slice holds ten or twenty billion switches.
Two Beijings... and I carry that around in my pocket every day?
Hold on. We're heading home.
Woohoo, homeward bound!

Let me check. Below, ten or twenty billion switches have no moving parts. Electric fields control whether they conduct. Above, over a dozen wiring layers connect them like a city. It's all face-down inside that black package. Right?
Exactly. You've got it.
...But wait. If all they can do is turn on and off, how do they figure out that one plus one is two?
Ah, that's for next time. We'll head back in and find out.

notes.title: 怎么用
items: 点进度条或下面的卡片跳到那一镜；播放时大图换成当前镜头的故事板，下方显示正在说的台词。
全片 10:27.0，58 镜；每镜时长 = 起势 + 台词 + 句间停顿 + 收尾，取整秒、不少于 4 秒。
配音只是听感预览（AI 合成），不进成片；改台词或时长后重跑 `python tools/audio_preview.py build` 即更新。
